papers.title: DAS reveals continuous, multicore architecture of the Alpine Fault, New Zealand
papers.abstract: The Alpine Fault accommodates much of the relative motion between the Australian and Pacific plates in southern New Zealand and is expected to produce large earthquakes in coming decades. How slip evolves and what ground motions are produced during the next rupture are expected to depend strongly on the continuity of principal slip zones and overall fault width. Despite extensive study, the along-strike structure of the fault and its continuity across segment boundaries remain poorly constrained. Here, we use distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) along a 30-kilometer fiber-optic array crossing the Alpine Fault to record fault-zone guided waves (FZGWs) from local earthquakes. The FZGW observations, supported by numerical modeling and passive seismic imaging, reveal up to six narrow (∼10 meters) fault cores embedded within a 200-meter-wide low-velocity zone interpreted as the fault’s inner damage zone. The principal fault core feature persists for ∼180 kilometers along strike between the Central and South Westland segments, crossing a pronounced geometric and kinematic boundary. The inferred damage zone width is consistent with empirical scaling for large-displacement faults. These results demonstrate that DAS can resolve fault-zone architecture at previously inaccessible scales and bridge geological and geophysical inferences, providing constraints on fault continuity, slip localization, and the potential for multisegment rupture in mature plate-boundary systems.

papers.title: Arctic forcing of European spring productivity and agricultural yields linked to Barents Sea ice loss
papers.abstract: Arctic sea ice loss reshapes midlatitude climate, yet its cascading impacts on terrestrial carbon cycling and food security remain unclear. Barents Sea ice area (BSIA) has experienced the Arctic’s fastest decline. Using four decades of satellite observations, agricultural statistics, and Earth system model (ESM) simulations, we identify late-winter BSIA as a key driver of European spring productivity. Interannual BSIA reductions substantially enhance gross primary productivity (GPP) and raise national wheat yields by up to 16.5% in Eastern Europe, a global breadbasket. Reanalysis and model experiments reveal that reduced BSIA alters large-scale circulation through stratosphere-troposphere coupling, wave–mean flow interactions, and Rossby wave propagation. Anomalous subsidence drives adiabatic and radiative warming; cyclonic flow strengthens warm-air advection, together alleviating thermal constraints on photosynthesis. Although most ESMs capture atmospheric teleconnections, they systematically underestimate productivity responses due to underrepresented GPP-temperature sensitivity. BSIA decline accounts for approximately half of the four-decade increase in Eastern European productivity, highlighting an overlooked Arctic forcing of midlatitude carbon dynamics.

Pyrethroid insecticide exposure enhances the ability of Helicoverpa armigera to counter host plant defenses through symbiotic bacteria
papers.abstract: Like plant toxins, synthetic insecticides can exert strong selective pressures on pest populations. While responses to both plant toxins and synthetic insecticides can depend on adaptive changes in the nuclear genotype of the pest species, increasing evidence suggests that symbiotic microbes, particularly gut microbes, can also influence these responses. In the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera , concentrations of the symbiont Corynebacterium glyciniphilum increased in moth strains that were treated with the pyrethroid pesticide lambda-cyhalothrin (LCH), and they were also high in LCH-resistant strains and in populations exposed to 2-Tridecanone (2-TD), a secondary defense compound that is present in the Solanaceae. This increase enhanced the ability of H. armigera to overcome not only the pesticide but also a key defense mechanism in the solanaceous plants. In field populations of H. armigera , the abundance of C. glyciniphilum was lowest in populations feeding on nonsolanaceous plants that were sensitive to LCH. Based on gene knockouts, the underlying reason for the enhanced defensive capability provided by C. glyciniphilum was attributed to two detoxification enzyme genes (a P450 cytochrome and an esterase ) which can metabolize both LCH and 2-TD into nontoxic degradation products. These findings suggest that a common mechanism mediated by a symbiont contributes to the insect’s capacity to develop resistance to both a pesticide and a host plant toxin.

papers.title: A novel family of polysaccharide lyase proteins are deployed in rice to negatively control arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis
papers.abstract: Abstract As the core structure of arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) symbiosis, arbuscules exhibit an unusually short lifespan, yet the underlying mechanisms remain largely obscure. In this study, a novel family of bacteria-originated polysaccharide lyases (designated chitin-binding and lyase proteins, CBLPs) was investigated in rice. After inoculation with the AM fungus Rhizophagus irregularis, OsCBLP1 was specifically induced in arbusculated cells while OsCBLP2 was expressed in both arbusculated and adjacent cells. Loss-of-function of either OsCBLP1 or OsCBLP2 resulted in enhanced root colonization, and the double mutant oscblp1 oscblp2 exhibited an even more exaggerated phenotype, indicating that the two OsCBLPs act additively to negatively regulate AM symbiosis. Overexpression of OsCBLPs significantly decreased arbuscule abundance in rice and Medicago truncatula roots. Both OsCBLPs were localized to the apoplastic space after plasmolysis, and purified OsCBLP1 not only efficiently bound and lysed chitin but also significantly inhibited hyphal elongation of germinated R. irregularis spores. Moreover, OsCBLP2 was induced in rice leaves during symbiosis and conferred effective resistance to the blast fungus. Together, this work reveals a common set of polysaccharide lyase genes that are used by plants to control both symbiotic and pathogenic fungi. It also indicates that arbuscule degradation is likely a consequence of active host defense.

papers.title: Interploidy massively increases meiotic crossovers in pericentromeric recombination deserts
papers.abstract: Meiotic recombination reshuffles genetic diversity through reciprocal DNA exchanges between chromosomes known as crossovers. In most eukaryotes, crossovers are highly constrained in both frequency and distribution, leaving large genomic regions with little or no recombination. A notable exception is the Brassica AAC allotriploid hybrid obtained from a cross between allotetraploid Brassica napus (AACC) and diploid Brassica rapa (AA), which exhibits elevated recombination and crossover formation near centromeres. Here, we generated a CCA allotriploid hybrid from a cross between B. napus and Brassica oleracea (CC), and subsequently produced AAC allotriploids by crossing the CCA hybrid with B. rapa . Both CCA and AAC allotriploids exhibit similar meiotic deregulation, demonstrating that this phenomenon is not restricted to AAC hybrids. Both systems displayed a marked increase in crossover frequency within normally low-recombining chromosome regions, reaching 9.4-fold in AAC and 13.4-fold in CCA allotriploids. Alternating CCA and AAC allotriploids efficiently reshuffled both B. napus subgenomes within only two generations. Using genetic mapping and cytogenetics, we further identified homoeologous exchanges. Remarkably, crossovers occurring on chromosomes involved in homoeologous associations exhibited a more pronounced redistribution toward nonrecombining regions than those on homologously paired chromosomes. Moreover, the frequency of homoeologous associations varied with the diploid progenitor genotype, indicating that genetic factors controlling homoeologous recombination already exist in Brassica diploids. Altogether, our results identify allotriploidy as a simple and powerful strategy to unlock recombination deserts, which harbor 21% of total resistance gene analogs, and provide insights into its potential role in allopolyploid evolution, adaptation, and speciation.

papers.title: A herbivore-induced plant volatile facilitates group foraging in locusts
papers.abstract: Plants have evolved sophisticated defense strategies against herbivory, often releasing volatile compounds upon attack to deter further feeding. Here, we demonstrate the induced volatile S-linalool promotes phase- and stage-specific group foraging in the migratory locust ( Locusta migratoria ). We show that S-linalool, a volatile whose emission increases more than 10-fold following damage by gregarious nymphs, acts as a potent attractant that drives other nymphs to aggregate and feed on previously attacked rice plants. Mechanistically, we identified the olfactory receptor LmOR49 that detects S-linalool and used genome editing to make this receptor nonfunctional, thereby abolishing both electrophysiological responses and behavioral attraction. We also inactivated rice genes required for S-linalool biosynthesis, abolishing its emission, rendering plants unattractive, and disrupting locust feeding preference. Although feeding on previously attacked plants provides no detectable direct fitness benefit under our experimental conditions, prior locust feeding suppresses the accumulation of deterrent metabolites, potentially increasing plant palatability for subsequent feeding. S-linalool thus serves as an olfactory cue that guides gregarious nymphs toward previously attacked, more palatable plants. Collectively, these findings uncover a comprehensive mechanism whereby a plant defense volatile is exploited by an insect herbivore to promote group foraging, broadening our understanding of plant–insect interactions and suggesting molecular targets for locust control.

papers.title: Soil contamination and acidification jointly increased cereal cadmium and dietary exposure over four decades
papers.abstract: Cadmium contamination of staple cereals is an important food-safety concern, yet how long-term changes in soil chemistry alter cadmium transfer into food remains poorly resolved. Here we reconstructed changes in cropland topsoil cadmium and pH across China from 1980 to 2020 and quantified their consequences for cereal grain cadmium, dietary exposure, and mitigation potential. National mean topsoil cadmium increased from 0.123 to 0.236 mg kg −1 , while mean cropland pH declined from 6.50 to 6.30 nationally and by about 0.5 units in several southern rice-growing provinces. These coupled changes increased mean grain cadmium from 0.043 to 0.100 mg kg −1 in rice and from 0.017 to 0.032 mg kg −1 in wheat. By 2020, provinces with estimated mean hazard quotients exceeded 1.0 had a combined population of about 138 million. Counterfactual analysis showed that soil cadmium accumulation remained the dominant driver of rising grain cadmium, while acidification substantially amplified soil-to-grain transfer, especially in rice systems. Scenario analysis to 2050 indicated that restoring cropland pH to 6.5 could offset about 44% of the projected increase in rice cadmium even without immediate source control, whereas combining pH restoration with source control reduced mean rice cadmium by about 59% and brought exceedance close to zero. These findings identify soil acidification as an important amplifier of cadmium transfer into staple cereals and highlight targeted cropland pH restoration as a practical near-term strategy for reducing food-chain exposure while longer-term source-control measures take effect.

papers.title: Structural basis of plastid Mg 2+ transport by the magnesium channel MGT10 in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Magnesium ions (Mg 2+ ) are vital for photosynthesis, serving as central metal ions in chlorophyll molecules and activating RuBisCO. MGT10 is the only member of the CorA/MRS2 superfamily bound to the chloroplast envelope membrane, where it mediates Mg 2+ uptake and homeostasis in chloroplasts. Despite its importance, the mechanism of MGT10-mediated Mg 2+ transport remains unclear. Here, we report cryoelectron microscopy structures of Arabidopsis MGT10 in two conformations, along with functional characterizations. MGT10 assembles into a homopentameric structure with a central tunnel connecting the transmembrane and soluble domains. A constriction ring consisting of five conserved arginine residues arranged asymmetrically in the tunnel is crucial for Mg 2+ conduction. Our structures reveal an unexpected gating mechanism involving a conformational transition from a symmetric closed state to an asymmetric, putatively open state. In addition, we identified an intramolecular disulfide bond within each soluble domain as a unique structural feature of MGT10. Structural and functional analyses show that this disulfide bond is required for MGT10’s structural integrity and for regulating its function in photosynthesis. Taken together, our findings provide insights into Mg 2+ transport and regulatory mechanisms of MGT10 in chloroplasts.

papers.title: Host control of rhizobial proliferation in soybean nodules
Foliar and floral frost damage reshape reproductive phenology with limited carry-over effects
papers.abstract: Abstract Late spring frost is an intensifying climatic disturbance, yet how frost damage to different organs (leaves and flowers) reshapes reproductive phenology and generates carry-over effects remains unclear. Using 259,732 phenological observations across eight European woody species spanning 1950–2024, we show that foliar frost damage shortened the fruit development period (FDP; the interval from flowering to fruit maturity) by 1.6 days, driven by delayed flowering and advanced fruit maturity. Conversely, floral frost damage prolonged FDP by 1.3 days through delayed fruit maturity, with both effects strengthening under greater frost severity. Accounting for anomalously warm conditions in the frost year substantially reduced the estimated delays in flowering and subsequent-year phenology, indicating that neglecting climatic context leads to overestimation of frost effects. These findings reveal organ-specific pathways through which frost damage reshapes reproductive phenology while generating limited carry-over effects, refining current understanding of phenological responses under climate change.

papers.title: The Plant Cell welcomes 2027 Assistant Features Editors
Biosynthesis of iboga alkaloids
papers.abstract: Abstract Tabernanthe iboga (iboga) is the source of voacangine, which is widely used as a semi-synthetic starting material for the anti-addiction agent ibogaine. Despite extensive investigation of voacangine biosynthesis, production of this compound cannot be reconstituted in a heterologous host, suggesting that one or more enzymes required for biosynthesis are missing. Additionally, T. iboga produces ibophyllidine, a pyrroloindole alkaloid that utilizes the same upstream precursor as voacangine, but is a member of a structurally distinct alkaloid class. Here we use bulk and single cell gene expression from leaf and root tissue to identify the unknown enzymes from these two pathways. We identify two additional enzymes that enable biosynthesis of voacangine in a heterologous host. The missing enzymes includes a pathogenesis-related (PR)10 family protein that likely catalyzes cyclization of a transient intermediate. Careful analysis of gene expression profiles in leaf and root also enabled the discovery of four additional enzymes that convert an upstream intermediate to ibophyllidine. This work reveals the chemical logic that generates two distinct alkaloid scaffolds in this important medicinal plant.

papers.title: Dual Pathways Mediate Blue Light Signaling-Regulated Melatonin Accumulation in Tomato Fruits
papers.abstract: Abstract Melatonin is an antioxidant and growth regulator in plants that directly or indirectly influences the yield and quality of vegetable crops. Melatonin accumulation is highly sensitive to light signals. Nevertheless, the biosynthetic route responsible for light response, along with its underlying regulatory architecture, remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that blue light stimulates the expression of SlASMT7, which encodes an enzyme in the "serotonin–5-methoxytryptamine" melatonin biosynthetic pathway, while also repressing melatonin catabolism via SlM2H. Both effects are mediated by the transcription factor SlHY5. SlHY5 activates SlASMT7 by directly binding to its promoter, whereas it represses SlM2H expression by recruiting histone deacetylases SlHDA4 and SlHDA8. Melatonin accumulation is temporally phased—biosynthesis predominates at the breaker stage, whereas SlM2H-mediated catabolism drives its decline and is accompanied by a stage-dependent metabolic transition. The HY5–ASMT7–M2H module shows consistent directional trends across multiple fleshy fruit species, suggesting possible evolutionary conservation. Together, these findings define a blue light-regulated pathway that links transcriptional and epigenetic control to melatonin homeostasis and metabolic reprogramming, providing a molecular framework for improving fruit quality through breeding and light management.

papers.title: A Super-Enhancer-Like Element and a Positive Feedback Loop Drive Ultra-High Expression of CCS for Red Pepper Ripening
papers.abstract: Abstract The capsanthin-capsorubin synthase (CCS) gene drives red pigment accumulation in pepper fruit through a ripening-specific transcriptional surge. In the pericarp of mature fruit, it is the second most highly expressed gene; however, the regulatory basis for this exceptional activation remains poorly understood. Here, we identified a super-enhancer-like (SE-like) element in the pepper (Capsicum annuum) CCS gene (CaCCS) promoter, composed of 22 tandem repeats partitioned into three groups by two intervening miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) insertions. MITE-associated siRNAs and DNA methylation suggest a potential role for these insertions in CaCCS repression before ripening, whereas CaDML2-mediated demethylation alleviates promoter repression during ripening. CArG-box motifs present in all repeats mediate CaRIN–CaTAGL1 activation of CaCCS in a copy number-dependent manner. Mechanistically, CaRIN binds and stabilizes CaTAGL1, and the resulting heteromeric complex activates the CaRIN promoter, establishing an autoregulatory positive feedback loop that amplifies CaRIN accumulation during ripening. CaRIN further undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation through its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region, forming nuclear condensates that are enriched at the CaCCS promoter and contain CaTAGL1. This study reveals how an SE-like cis-element, MITEs-directed epigenetic dynamics, and a self-reinforcing CaRIN–CaTAGL1 transcriptional circuit and biomolecular condensates work together to drive the ripening-specific increase in CaCCS expression. Our findings reveal the regulatory mechanisms through which quantitative and temporal control of gene expression underlies metabolic innovation in Capsicum species.

papers.title: Steering nanometric reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycle for PFAS mineralization
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), known as “forever chemicals,” have highly stable C─F bonds that render them resistant to destruction by conventional water treatment processes. Here, we developed a destructive technology that does not require external photo-, electro-, or heat energy input, relying simply on Fenton-like cycles (peroxymonosulfate activation) under nanometric spatial confinement. Unlike the ordinary activation process, confinement shielded peroxymonosulfate radicals ( S O 5 • − ) from external quenching and enabled them to remain active for reductive defluorination. Coupled with oxidative sulfate radicals ( S O 4 • − ), this process unlocked a synergistic “reduction-oxidation” destruction pathway. Specifically, the catalyst was designed by planting single-atom cobalt on MXene nanosheets, whose interlaminar confinement directed efficient PFAS mineralization via alternating α-carbon defluorination (by S O 5 • − ) and decarbonization (by S O 4 • − ). We further constructed a Fenton bed that allowed highly efficient and cost-effective treatment of PFASs in complex water matrices. Our findings underscore the promising potential of nanoconfinement in driving reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycles toward efficient PFAS mineralization.
